query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex, initially single-phase high-entropy alloys, cyclic mechanical loading combined with elevated temperatures can drive localized grain-boundary segregation that nucleates nanoscale intermetallic precipitates, thereby triggering a transition to brittle behavior unlike that seen in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with uniform grain-boundary composition.
generation.intervention: Application of cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures compared to static or low-temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under cyclic loading and thermal exposure that mimic service conditions likely to promote solute segregation, contrasted with static loading or lower temperature controls.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized grain-boundary segregation leading to the formation of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Cyclic stress and elevated temperature induce thermodynamically driven compositional fluctuations at grain boundaries, promoting nucleation of brittle intermetallic phases that serve as crack initiation sites and impair toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to cyclic loading at higher temperatures will exhibit measurable grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitate formation, accompanied by a significant reduction in fracture toughness relative to baseline and static conditions.
generation.baseline: Initial microstructure with homogeneous composition and no detectable nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be most pronounced under conditions of cyclic loading and elevated temperature; if the alloy is operated under static conditions or at sufficiently low temperatures, the anticipated brittle transformation may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in toughness and the critical loading/temperature parameters required to trigger segregation and precipitate formation remain to be experimentally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the high-entropy alloy and subject one set to cyclic loading at elevated temperatures while maintaining a control set under static loading or low-temperature conditions. Characterize the grain-boundary chemistry and microstructure using high-resolution microscopy and atom probe tomography, and assess fracture toughness using standardized mechanical tests.
measurements: Presence and morphology of nanoscale precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cyclically loaded, high-temperature samples do not show statistically significant increases in grain-boundary segregation, intermetallic precipitate formation, or a reduction in fracture toughness compared to controls, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

recalled_precedents.approach: They employed advanced microscopy (atom probe tomography, TEM) and mechanical testing on high‐entropy alloys to correlate subtle solute segregation at grain boundaries with variations in toughness, contrasting with conventional alloys.
recalled_precedents.finding: They observed that even small levels of elemental segregation could nucleate nanoscale precipitates under stress or thermal exposure that degraded fracture toughness, suggesting a stress‐assisted compositional instability.

recalled_precedents.study: Gao et al. (circa 2016, Progress in Materials Science)
recalled_precedents.approach: A combined computational and experimental investigation was used, where the authors studied intermetallic nucleation in compositionally complex alloys under varied thermal and mechanical histories.
recalled_precedents.finding: They found that while a single‐phase microstructure can be initially stabilized by high configurational entropy, mechanical or thermal stimuli can drive local compositional fluctuations that lead to brittle intermetallic formation along defect sites.

recalled_precedents.approach: This work implemented controlled loading experiments comparing high‐entropy alloys subjected to cyclic fatigue versus static annealing, with microstructural characterization via high‐resolution TEM and atom probe analysis.
recalled_precedents.finding: They demonstrated that under cyclic loading, even nominally single‐phase high-entropy alloys developed localized nanoscale phase separations at grain-boundary triple junctions, correlating with a pronounced drop in toughness.
